title: The Long Way Home
intro: Marta Vess vanished from the Halvorsen Ridge research station in January. The snow kept the ridge the way glass keeps a face, and her footprints across the yard show exactly where she stopped: mid-stride, one print ahead of the other, nothing behind it. No drag marks. No second set of tracks. The search parties found her coat on its hook and her tea gone cold in its mug, and they closed the file by spring.

What the file does not hold is the W-calibration log left open on her desk. A personal shift, it records, tested once in the yard, at small scale. The coordinates slide steadily off-grid, along a fourth axis that is not a metaphor and was never supposed to be measurable. She did not disappear from the world. She left it in a direction the world does not have a word for.

Since then the station has begun to fold. Rooms slide out of line with one another along that same axis, and the instruments can see it now, where before only Marta's log claimed it. The route she took is still there, the way a tide leaves a route in sand. This is the account of walking it.

before: You came back to the station in winter, when there was nobody left to stop you. The doors still shut. The heat still works. Nobody has told the building otherwise, and it carries on with its routines out of habit, the way a house creaks at the same hour every night.

The fold begins here, in the corridor between the boiler room and the radio room, which has become too long. Rooms have slid out of line along an axis the instruments can read and the eye cannot name. Marta's calibration log sits open on the console, its margins annotated in her careful hand. You set the dials. You learn to step sideways through the world.
after: The first shift ends with your knees on a floor that should be a wall. The world settles, and a room you passed a hundred times is standing there where the wall used to be. Nothing in you accepts this, and everything under your ribs already believes it.

A page torn from the log is propped on the console, weighted with a spanner against the draught. It reads: the station did not break; I unfolded it. Sorry. I am only testing how far back it goes. The handwriting does not shake. That is the part you keep returning to, standing in the room that used to be a wall.

before: The fold has spread since the corridor. Now it reaches the lift, a cast-iron car the station has trusted for forty years. It hangs in its shaft, oscillating along W, hissing up and down an axis it has no business having, and the sound it makes is the sound of a rope being worked over a ledge.

The mechanics' landing that should be here has slid away, and the far stair has collapsed under the ice, so the shaft is the only way down. The car passes the opening at intervals. Its rhythm is wrong, but it is a rhythm, and wrong rhythms can still be learned.
after: You wait at the shaft mouth until the count lives in your chest, then step in at the half-second where the car is still in every axis at once. The ride is a silence between two worlds. It lets you out on a landing that exists only while you are standing on it.

On the car's ceiling, in grease pencil, in the handwriting of a man who did not stop to wonder: if it moves and you can't see it move, it's moving the wrong way. Ride the pause. Beneath it, smaller, a date and a checkmark, as if the man had tried it himself and survived the trying, and wanted the next rider to know.

before: The workshop now holds two rooms in one footprint. Yours sits at W. Marta's house stands at W+2, occupying the same air, its lamp still on, its door facing a garden that grows through your workbench. The overlap is not an illusion. The kettle in its kitchen is three years into the same boil.

The log says she kept her private papers at home rather than at the station, and that the house counts as home even when it stands where you are standing. To read what she wrote, you will have to walk through her wall, and mean it.
after: You cross into the house and touch nothing. Her coat is still on its hook, one sleeve brushed by the same page of your calendar that hangs from your own nail. The notes are where a person hides things in their own house: under the boards, behind the clock, in the tin of old batteries.

You read them where she wrote them, at her table. One sentence from the last page stays with you on the way out: I keep thinking the fourth axis is not a direction. It is a room we have never been allowed to turn around in.

before: Below the station, the undercroft went down with the first winter of the fold. The old storerooms lie under their own rubble, and the stone stair ends in a blocked dark that no shovel will open. But the log gives the undercroft a W of its own, deeper the further down it goes.

Her margin note is nearly diagram and nearly joke: to reach the far end, climb. The ladder out of the ruin runs along the fourth axis, each rung above the last in a direction no ladder has ever stood up into. You will descend the whole way and never stop going down.
after: The climb feels like falling, and the falling feels like coming home, and you learn not to argue with either. The last rung lets you out into air that has never once been inside the station, cold and faintly salt, moving in a slow tide through the walls.

Somebody has scratched into a roof beam with something too blunt to be a knife: whatever is down here, it isn't trapped. I think it was patient before we were. The scratches are old and the dust has partly filled them, but the beam they cross is one the log says was set in place last century, in a room nobody has opened since.

before: You surface onto the ridge field where the glass grows. Pillars of it, thin as reeds, set in the frozen ground at no pattern you can find, and each one oscillates along W until it blurs, like a struck note trying to stand still. In the wind they ring, low and unhurried, the way a bridge talks to itself in weather.

Her route home runs along the far edge of the field, and her log surveys it: numbered waypoints between the pillars, distances in her precise small hand. The numbers run out partway down the field, where the survey becomes something else. You pick up her old tracks and keep them under your boots.
after: Somewhere past the last numbered waypoint, her beacon comes into view through the fold, a coal that does not gutter. The distance between you and it keeps rearranging itself, and each waypoint sets you nearer than the last, as though the field were stepping toward you too.

You stop where her tracks stop. She stopped here mid-stride, one print ahead of the other. The glass around you hums one held chord, then lets it go, and you walk on through the place where a person used to be.

before: The fold opens at the end of the ridge. It is not a door and it is not a light; it is a long way, a route made visible, a distance that has stood up on its edge. Every axis leans toward it. The station behind you has gone quiet, as if it were listening.

Her beacon burns at the far end, steady as a porch lamp left for someone expected. The last waypoint in her log lies here, where the last glass pillar stands ringing softly. You set your pack down. You pick up her stride and match it, and you go the long way home.
after: The fold takes you the way deep water takes a stone, without hurry and without asking. The ringing of the glass fades along an axis you now feel rather than see, and what replaces it is the ordinary sound of snow, and of your own breathing keeping step with something.

At the last waypoint, on a stone she has squared and set upright, one line is cut deep enough to survive any weather: the long way home is not far. It is only wide. Come the way I came and the door will know you.

epilogue: You find Marta in the fold, thin and steady, her watch thirty years ahead of yours and her hair the same as ever, which is its own kind of answer. She looks at you the way people look at a door left open, then she asks if the kettle has been emptied. You say yes. You both know it is a strange first thing to say, and you let it be strange, and it holds.

You shift home together, one waypoint at a time along her surveyed route, her stride and yours matched print for print. The fold closes behind you without sound. The station stands on the ridge exactly as buildings do when they have finished saying what they came to say, and the snow keeps the yard the way glass keeps a face.

At night, in your own kitchen, you sit with her log open to its final page, the one you have not shown anyone. It says: we are not the first things to learn the way back. Something else knows it, and it has been leaving the door unlocked for us. I think it wants company. You close the book. The kettle ticks as it cools, and the house is quiet in a way it was not before you went after her.
